newsitem.title: USA: Albright discusses Mideast peace with Levy.
newsitem.headline: Albright discusses Mideast peace with Levy.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright discussed the stalled Middle East peace process with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy on Friday amid hints that Washington may trim aid to Israel in favour of Jordan.

Speaking to reporters, Albright stressed Washington's desire to reward Jordan for its peace efforts and did not deny that the money might come out of the traditional hefty annual U.S. aid allocation for the Jewish state.
Israel Radio reported on Thursday that U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, on a trip to the region, had raised the issue of a possible $50 million cut in U.S. aid in talks with Israeli officials.
Albright said no conclusion had so far been reached on how to help Jordan and said the administration would consult with the U.S. Congress, which approves aid, on any decision.

Albright also made clear she had no intention of personally visiting the Middle East until the Israelis and Palestinians made "difficult decisions" to move forward their peace talks, which have been stalled for two months.
Ross was returning to Washington on Friday after talks which he has described as "useful," and will report to President Bill Clinton and Albright.
Albright said the United States had been looking for some time for ways to step up aid to Jordan "and the other friends of peace in the Middle East."
She said Clinton had discussed the issue with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who shared an interest in establishing what she called "a fund for Middle East peace and security."
"We are now examining with the Israelis details on how best to move forward on this, and when we reach a conclusion on this we'll be consulting with Congress," she said.

Levy said that "aid to Jordan is a mutual desire of the United States and Israel. It's an important link to strengthen the peace process. I'm sure we will find a common way in order to achieve this goal."

Israel receives about $3 billion annually from the United States and Egypt some $2 billion. Jordan received just $47 million economic and military aid in 1997 and Clinton asked for $75.6 million in his 1998 budget request.
The administration believes Jordan has shown steadfast devotion to the peace process in difficult circumstances, without receiving significant economic benefits so far.

Albright said the United States would do what it could to push forward the peace process, which has halted over the issue of Jewish housing construction in East Jerusalem and the West Bank, but the main responsibility lay with the parties.
"It is actually the two parties that have to come together. It is the two parties that have to make the difficult decisions here," she said.
"I will go (to the Middle East) when the time is ripe and when the parties are prepared to make some of the decisions that are really required," she added.
Levy, apparently indicating that difficulties remained ahead, said: "We have to fulfil all agreements, but also to curb the expectations."
In Cairo, a spokesman for Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on Friday the Middle East peace process was "clinically dead" and urged the United States to resurrect it.
The spokesman, Marwan Kanafani, said Arafat had sent a letter to Clinton saying the president must act quickly to save the peace process.
